summary: Lays out the general definitions and mechanisms for creating new URN namespaces, which are a way to give permanent names to things. It is a Best Current Practice and was replaced by RFC 3406.

eli5.summary: Before you can print a new kind of name tag, you need rules on who may make them. This document gave the rules for making them.

subtitle: The rules and template for creating a new URN namespace and getting its Namespace ID from IANA.

tldr.problem: Uniform Resource Names need managed namespaces, but there was no common process for turning a collection of identifiers into a valid URN namespace.
tldr.mechanism: A registrant fills in a standard definition template and gets a Namespace ID (NID) through one of three registration categories: Experimental, Informal or Formal.
tldr.outcome: This Best Current Practice (BCP 33) has been obsoleted by RFC 3406, which now holds the namespace definition rules.

today: RFC 2611 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 33) that has been obsoleted by RFC 3406, which now holds the URN namespace definition mechanisms.

sections.title: Managed URN Namespaces
sections.content:
RFC 2611 follows the URN syntax defined in RFC 2141. Uniform Resource Names (URNs) identify a resource independent of its location and are meant to last. The memo rests on two assumptions. First, assigning a URN is a managed process, so not every string that matches the URN syntax is a valid URN. Second, the space of URN namespaces is managed, so a namespace needs a recognized definition to be valid.

The memo gives a template for defining a namespace and a way to get an identifier for it, the Namespace ID (NID), registered with IANA. It only covers creating namespaces. If URNs in a namespace should be resolvable, a separate registration in a global NID directory such as the NAPTR system is needed.
sections.eli5: Not every made-up name counts as an official name. This memo explains how a group can get its own official type of name.

sections.title: What a URN Namespace Is
sections.content:
A namespace is a collection of uniquely assigned identifiers. The namespace's own identifier keeps URNs globally unique and can hint at the structure of the identifier. The memo's example is that ISBNs and ISSNs are both publishing identifiers, and a number could be valid in both, so separate designators keep the URNs distinct.

How the identifiers are built, assigned and used depends on the community that defines them, and that is outside the scope of the IETF URN work. This document covers only how such a collection becomes a real URN namespace by obtaining a NID.
sections.eli5: School ID numbers and library card numbers could look alike. Writing which kind it is in front keeps them from being confused.

sections.title: The Definition Template
sections.content:
A namespace is defined by filling in a template. It is designed to help both those seeking URNs in the namespace and those who want to run resolvers. The fields are:

  • Namespace ID, assigned by IANA, with registration version number and a registration date in YYYY-MM-DD form
  • The declared registrant (name and e-mail required)
  • Declaration of syntactic structure and relevant ancillary documentation
  • Identifier uniqueness and persistence considerations
  • Process of identifier assignment and process for identifier resolution
  • Rules for lexical equivalence and conformance with URN syntax
  • Validation mechanism and scope

Uniqueness means an identifier is assigned to at most one resource and never reassigned. Resolution in a global scheme needs registration in a Resolution Discovery System (RDS) such as NAPTR. Characters reserved in URN syntax are normally handled by hex encoding. The scope section matters when judging a requested NID: a namespace for "social security numbers" should be global, while a national one can claim just that nation's numbers.
sections.eli5: It is a form with questions: who owns this kind of name, how are names made, can two things get the same name, and who is allowed to hand them out.

sections.title: Registration Categories
sections.content:
Three categories of URN namespace are defined, with different levels of disclosure and review.

  • Experimental: not registered with IANA, written X-<NID>. Nothing prevents collisions, so they are for internal or limited use.
  • Informal: registered with IANA, with an NID of the form urn-<number> chosen First Come First Served. The registrant sends the completed template to the urn-nid mailing list for a 2 week discussion, then submits it to IANA.
  • Formal: processed through an RFC review, not necessarily on the standards track, after a 2 week discussion on the list. The NID is assigned by IETF consensus.

A formal NID must not already be registered, must not start with x- or urn-, must not start with two ASCII letters followed by a hyphen, and must be more than 2 letters long. All two-letter combinations are reserved for possible country-code based NIDs.

Because URNs should persist, few changes should be made to how URN strings are interpreted. Informal registrations are updated by the registrant through the same discussion process, and formal ones by updating the RFC, with a 2 week review on the list.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to get a name type: scribble a quick one for your own use, sign up on the club list, or get the whole group to formally agree.

sections.title: The Worked Example
sections.content:
The memo includes a filled-in template for a hypothetical "generic Internet namespace" discussed informally in the URN working group. Its identifiers look like URN:<assigned number>:<FQDN>:<assigned US-ASCII string>, where the fully qualified domain name is delegated to the domain name holder, who assigns the string.

The memo itself warns that this is a poor URN namespace in practice, because domain names can be reassigned, which breaks uniqueness. It is shown only to illustrate the template and is not proposed seriously.

The Security Considerations section notes that the declarations are public and low risk, but there is a danger of spoofing and misinformation, so the information should be taken as advisory.
sections.eli5: The example fills in the form for a pretend name type built on website names. The authors admit it is a bad idea, because website names can change hands.
